sources.title: Cree Nation Government, The Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee
sources.note: Sections “The Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee” and “Cree First Nation Communities”: Eeyou self-name, People’s Land, eleven affiliated communities, more than 300 family hunting territories, and independently administered First Nations.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Governance and Structure
sources.note: Opening paragraphs say the Grand Council and Cree Nation Government together “represent the coming together of the executive and administrative branches of Cree government” serving Eeyouch in eastern James Bay and southeastern Hudson Bay.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Agreements
sources.note: Sections on the 1975 JBNQA, 2002 Paix des Braves, 2010 offshore agreement, 2012 territorial governance, and 2017 Cree Nation Governance Agreement distinguish modern institutions and legal geographies.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Timeline: The Crees of Yesterday and Today
sources.note: Dated milestones from 1971 onward document hydroelectric impacts, Cree political action, the Grand Council, agreements, language legislation, and living nation-building.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Social and Cultural Development
sources.note: Mandate and responsibilities sections cover youth, Elders, women, language commission, place names, archaeology, land knowledge, public education, and partnerships.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Honouring the Ways of our ancestors
sources.note: Page dated 24 January 2022: Cree-Innu caribou understanding, elder-guided sharing, sustainable harvest, respect for animals, local authorization, and tallymen; dated modern stewardship, not a 1492 rulebook.

sources.title: Karine Neumann and Paul Wattez, Technical Note 3: Land Use
sources.note: PDF page 14, section 2.1: pre-contact small hunting groups, 4,200-year Broadback archaeology, summer fishing gatherings, and late-seventeenth-century posts; pages 2 and 19 to 20 explain consultation and sensitive family-camp data.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Research
sources.note: Sections “The Oujé-Bougoumou Archaeology Project,” “The km 13 Archaeological Site,” and “The Artifacts”: community collaboration, undated pre-contact stone-tool workshops, 5,865 artifacts from 30 square metres, local stone, and limited cultural attribution.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Learn
sources.note: Sections “Teacher Resources,” “Stories and Legends,” and “Elders”: school resources, workshops, orally transmitted history, captured stories, and elder guidance.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Family Weekend
sources.note: Page posted 29 October 2012: parents and children learned syllabics together, mothers and daughters sewed and beaded, and a Chisasibi healer discussed children’s rites of passage.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Footprints: A Walk Through Generations
sources.note: Single-page exhibit release: about 150 objects including snowshoes, moccasins, parkas, hunting and trapping tools, mittens, and children’s ceremonial outfits; materials display skill and artistry.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Something Good is Cooking!
sources.note: Page posted 4 October 2013: winter preparation, fish cleaning, a smoke dome, preserving fish and game, seasonal trout, visitors, and community participation.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, The trail of the Rabbit Fur Coat
sources.note: Page posted 14 March 2016: a Wemindji family object biography connects a rabbit-fur coat, camp foods, mittens and hat, family memories, makers, museum care, and intergenerational teaching.

sources.title: East Cree Language Resource Project, About
sources.note: Sections on two standardized dialects, stories, lessons, and dictionary: site begun in 2000, English-Cree dictionary first published in 2004, French-Cree in 2007, and continuing updates.

sources.title: Marie-Odile Junker and Marguerite MacKenzie, East Cree Dialects
sources.note: 2019 citation and opening sections name Northern and Southern East Cree, their different spelling conventions, community distributions, coastal and inland Southern varieties, and the transitional position of Eastmain.

sources.title: Eastern James Bay Cree Dictionary, nipii
sources.note: Exact modern dictionary entry gives Northern syllabics ᓂᐲ, roman spelling nipii, inanimate-noun class, and English definition “water.”

sources.title: Luci Bobbish Salt, Alice Duff, Linda Visitor, Marguerite MacKenzie, and Marie-Odile Junker, Spelling East Cree For Eastern James Bay Cree Syllabics (Northern Dialect)
sources.note: 2016 citation; “Introduction” and “Syllabic Finals” explain community spelling variation, small final symbols, ongoing standardization, and revisions incorporated into dictionaries from 2004 onward.

sources.title: Marie-Odile Junker (ed.), The Interactive East Cree Reference Grammar
sources.note: Landing page and supplied 2000 to 2019 citation distinguish Northern and Southern grammars, identify syllabics as the writing system, and link talking charts, sounds, spelling, and verb conjugations.

sources.title: East Cree Language Resource Project, Publications
sources.note: Dated community education resources include 2002 and 2004 dialect books, a 2009 syllabics workbook, dictionaries, conversation materials, stories, mathematics terminology, and literacy tools.

sources.title: Eastern James Bay Cree Dictionary, boat gloss
sources.note: Exact modern Northern and Southern entries include ᒌᒫᓐ chiimaan, glossed “boat, ship” and, at Waswanipi, “boat, barge; canoe.”

sources.title: Cree School Board, Our Story
sources.note: Opening and JBNQA sections distinguish family and land-based learning from imposed schooling, describe the 1975 agreement, and date Cree School Board constitution to 28 June 1978.

sources.title: Cree School Board, Annual Report 2019-2020 (English)
sources.note: Report page 19, “Cree Component Priorities”: Cree History and Citizenship, Cree Language curriculum, land-based programs, teacher training, literacy certification, and the Cree Elder Video project.

sources.title: Cree Health, Â uhtahîpânûhch nipii - Drinking Water Sources in Eeyou Istchee
sources.note: Published 9 April 2025 and updated 6 May 2026; “Recommendations for handling water from natural sources” and “Are all nipii (water) sources in Eeyou Istchee clean and safe?” cover containers, boiling, wastewater, and illness risk.

sources.title: E. Bobet, Summary Report on the Nituuchischaayihtitaau Aschii Multi-Community Environment-and-Health Study
sources.note: Abstract on the 2013 research-library page describes hunting, fishing, traditional foods, contaminants, drinking-water sources, animal-borne and water-borne illness risk, and community health priorities.

sources.title: Evert Nieboer, Éric Dewailly, Louise Johnson-Down, Hugues Sampasa-Kanyinga, Marie-Ludivine Château-Degat, Grace M. Egeland, Laura Atikessé, Elizabeth Robinson, and Jill Torrie, Nituuchischaayihtitaau Aschii Multi-community Environment-and-Health Study in Eeyou Istchee, 2005-2009: Final Technical Report
sources.note: PDF page 174, report page 156, section 8.1: rivers, lakes, springs, wells, snow, 1980s water and sewage systems, flush toilets, bush camps, contamination, and testing.

sources.title: Cree Health, Historic Milestone Achieved for Cree Midwifery in Eeyou Istchee
sources.note: Published 13 May 2025 and updated 11 September 2026; section “The EIPC Program: Fostering Cree Midwifery Leadership” combines equivalent professional competencies, cultural and traditional knowledge, remote-birth emergency skills, community education, and perinatal care.

sources.title: Cree Health, Nishiiyuu Department launches traditional medicine cards
sources.note: Published 10 August 2020 and updated 15 January 2025; opening paragraphs and “Traditional Medicines” credit knowledge keepers and identify balsam fir, cedar, sage, sweetgrass, tamarack, tobacco, and white spruce, with contacts for traditional healers or herbalists.

sources.title: C. Leduc, J. Coonishish, P. Haddad, and A. Cuerrier, Plants used by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee (Quebec, Canada) for the treatment of diabetes: A novel approach in quantitative ethnobotany
sources.note: Journal of Ethnopharmacology 105 (2006), pages 55 to 63; abstract reports interviews with 34 Cree Elders and 18 plant species associated with 15 diabetes-related symptoms in a modern, non-exhaustive survey.

sources.title: Cree Health, A celebration of Eeyou/Eenou Family Values
sources.note: Opening paragraphs and “Explore the values,” updated 15 January 2025: names Iiyiyiuiyihtuwin, the Eeyou/Eenou way of life, and connects family values with land, harvested foods, respect, gratitude, sharing, teaching, and child rearing.

sources.title: Cree Nation Government, Capital Works and Services
sources.note: Mission, role, and services explicitly include essential sanitation, housing inspection, and support for community drinking-water and wastewater treatment.

sources.title: Agreement Between the Crees of Eeyou Istchee and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada Concerning the Eeyou Marine Region
sources.note: Sections 8.2 to 8.3, 10.1 to 11.1, 18.5, 26.2, and Schedule 30-1 Part IV: planning, wildlife, harvesting, impact review, archaeology, and Cree-Inuit overlap institutions and rights.

sources.title: Colin Scott, Family Territories, Community Territories: Balancing Rights and Responsibilities through Time
sources.note: Anthropologica 60(1) (2018), pages 90 to 105; pages 90 to 98, especially “Historical Perspectives” and “Eeyou Hunting Law Today,” review authority, access, collective validation, travel, fishing, berry gathering, meat sharing, and modern written hunting law.

sources.title: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee)/Cree Nation Government, Annual Report 2024-2025, “Declaration: Affirming and Promoting the Rights of the Eeyou/Eenou Child”
sources.note: Declaration at printed pages 188 to 189, PDF pages 190 to 191; the enumerated rights on printed page 189, PDF page 191 affirm education and traditional knowledge, health and social services, participation in decisions, clean drinking water, protected lands and traditional foods, and accountable governments; explicitly contemporary.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Visit
sources.note: Sections “Main Collection Summary,” “Collection Database,” and “Acquisitions” describe a Cree-led museum, historical objects, community additions, and knowledge databases.

sources.title: François Guindon, Technical Note 4: Archaeology and Cultural Heritage Survey
sources.note: Printed page 23, PDF file page 29, section 4.1.2 “Late Paleohistory (2000 BP to 400 BP)”: southern and northern site patterns, summer gatherings, multi-family dwellings, waterside camps, fauna, stone, pottery, ochre, and caribou.
